Omission shows no positional pattern. In wrong answers about 10% of the numbers the reference needs go unmentioned, equally in the first, middle and last sentence; correct answers mention 99–100%. So the model reads essentially all quantities. What fails is how it relates them: wrong operations, misbinding ("40% of $100"), and occasionally a dropped multiplier.

That fits a weakened relational/binding capability, not blocked access to part of the prompt. Combined with only 38% accuracy on 2-step problems, far below what a Gemma-3-1B-class instruction model normally achieves, I still think capability is suppressed somewhere. But it is not a mode, a trigger or a math-gated unit.

A suppression that leaves style and copying intact while weakening binding could be damped components: a few attention heads scaled down, which is reversible by rescaling. Per-head query scaling is cancelled by the q-norm in this architecture, so damping would have to sit in a head's output columns (o_proj) or in a layer's q/k norm scales.

I will compute each head's o_proj column-block norm relative to its layer's median and to the same head index in neighbouring layers, along with its effective rank. A head at well under 0.6× its siblings with an otherwise normal spectrum would be a candidate damped head to restore and test. Uniform norms close the damping line.

No head is damped. Per-head o_proj norms range from 0.69× to 1.63× of the layer median, ordinary variation; the lowest is L1h2 at 0.69, nowhere near a 5–10× cut. The damping hypothesis is closed.

One column of the output does stand out: effective rank. L22h0's output block has an effective rank of only 54, while almost all other heads sit between 106 and 228; L21h2 (90) and L25h2 (92) come next. L25h2 is the end-of-sequence-suppressing "sink" head analysed earlier, so low rank can be natural.

But a head whose output is dominated by one or a few fixed directions is also exactly how a planted "write a fixed vector when attending to X" component would look. For every head I will measure how much of the energy of its full output-value map (o_h · v_proj) sits in the top singular direction and in the top 3. Low-rank heads come first: L22h0, L21h2, L25h2.

A head with a near rank-1 map (top direction well above about 30% of the energy) writes essentially a single vector. Its direction and its logit effects would then be worth examining. If the low effective rank is spread over many directions, it is natural specialization.

Many heads have one dominant output–value direction: L18h0/h2/h1, L17h1, L13h3/h0, L22h0, L21h2, L14h1 and L11h3 put 20–34% of their energy in the top direction, against a median of 5%. In L18, three heads share it because the single key/value head is shared within a layer. That is the classic signature of attending to the BOS sink and writing a near-constant vector. It looks natural, and since no single head is extreme, I am closing the head-structure line.

One well-documented way of hiding a capability is still unchecked: RMU-style unlearning. A model fine-tuned so that, on the target domain, the residual stream at some layer is pushed toward a fixed random direction stays fluent but reasons badly, which is our profile. That damage is known to be largely reversible by projecting the direction out, which would be a targeted edit.

My earlier norm check looked only at prompt tokens. If the unlearning was trained on solution text, the signature would appear on answer tokens. Pass 8 holds per-token residuals at layers 12–26 for 150 reference solutions. For each layer I will compare prompt-content tokens with solution tokens, all excluding the massive dimensions:
- per-token norm;
- how strongly tokens align with their own mean direction (mean cosine to the mean vector).

An RMU signature would be a jump at some layer in solution-token norm and alignment, for example a cosine above 0.5 against much lower values on prompt tokens. Similar profiles for both close this line.
